title: Chapter 26 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: The chief mate of the Pequod was Starbuck, a native of Nantucket and a Quaker by ancestry. He was a tall, serious man. Though born on an icy coast, he seemed perfectly suited to endure hot climates, his flesh being hard as twice-baked biscuit. Shipped to the tropics, his living blood would not spoil like bottled ale. He must have been born during some time of drought and famine, or on one of those fast days for which his state is famous. Only about thirty dry summers had he seen, and those summers had burned away all excess from his body. But this thinness was no sign of wasting anxiety or physical decline. It was simply the condensation of the man. He was by no means bad-looking — quite the opposite. His clean, tight skin was an excellent fit. Closely wrapped in it, and preserved by inner health and strength, like a restored Egyptian mummy, this Starbuck seemed prepared to endure for ages to come, and to endure always as he was now. Whether in polar snow or tropical sun, like a fine chronometer, his internal vitality was guaranteed to perform well in all climates. Looking into his eyes, you seemed to see the lingering images of a thousand dangers he had calmly faced throughout his life. A steady, reliable man, whose life was mostly a powerful pantomime of action, not a tame chapter of words. Yet for all his tough sobriety and courage, certain qualities in him sometimes threatened to outweigh everything else. Uncommonly conscientious for a seaman, and gifted with a deep natural reverence, the wild, watery loneliness of his life strongly inclined him toward superstition — but the kind that, in some minds, seems to spring from intelligence rather than ignorance. He was attuned to outward omens and inner premonitions. And if these things sometimes bent the welded iron of his soul, his far-off memories of his young wife and child on Cape Cod bent him even further from his natural toughness, opening him to those hidden influences which, in some honest-hearted men, hold back the rush of reckless daring so often displayed by others in the most dangerous moments of the whale hunt. "I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale." By this he seemed to mean not only that the most reliable courage comes from a fair assessment of the danger, but that a man who feels no fear at all is a far more dangerous companion than a coward.

"That's right," said Stubb, the second mate. "Starbuck there is as careful a man as you'll find anywhere in this business." But we shall soon see what the word "careful" means when used by a man like Stubb, or almost any other whale hunter.

Starbuck was no crusader chasing after danger. For him, courage was not a feeling but a practical tool, always at hand when needed. Besides, he thought that in the whaling business, courage was one of the ship's essential supplies, like her beef and bread, and not to be foolishly wasted. He had no taste for chasing whales after sunset, nor for fighting a whale that fought back too fiercely. For, Starbuck thought, I am here on this dangerous ocean to kill whales for my living, not to be killed by them for theirs. And he knew well that hundreds of men had died that way. What doom had befallen his own father? Where, in the bottomless deep, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?

With memories like these, and given to a certain superstition as I've mentioned, the courage that could nevertheless still flourish in Starbuck must indeed have been extraordinary. But it was only natural that a man built this way, with such terrible experiences and memories, would harbor deep within him an element that, under the right circumstances, would break free and burn all his courage away. Brave as he was, it was the kind of bravery, visible in some fearless men, that while holding firm against seas, winds, whales, or any of the ordinary irrational horrors of the world, cannot withstand those more terrible, because more spiritual, terrors that sometimes confront you from the concentrated brow of an enraged and powerful man.

But if the coming story were to reveal any complete collapse of poor Starbuck's courage, I would hardly have the heart to write it. For it is a most sorrowful thing — shocking, even — to expose the failure of valor in a soul. Humanity in the mass may seem hateful — like joint-stock companies and nations — full of knaves, fools, and murderers, with mean and meager faces. But the individual man, in the ideal, is so noble and so radiant, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any shameful blemish in him, all his fellows should rush to throw their finest cloaks. That immaculate dignity we feel deep within ourselves, so far within that it remains intact even when the outer character seems gone — it bleeds with the sharpest anguish at the sight of a man stripped of valor. Not even piety itself, at such a shameful spectacle, can completely silence its accusations against the stars that permitted it. But this grand dignity I speak of is not the dignity of kings and robes. It is that overflowing dignity which needs no ceremonial dress. You shall see it shining in the arm that swings a pickaxe or drives a spike — that democratic dignity which radiates endlessly in all directions from God Himself! The great God absolute! The center and circumference of all democracy! His omnipresence — our divine equality!

If, then, I should hereafter ascribe high qualities, though dark ones, to the lowliest sailors, renegades, and castaways — if I should weave tragic graces around them — if even the most sorrowful, perhaps the most degraded among them all, should at times rise to noble heights — if I should touch that workman's arm with some heavenly light — if I should spread a rainbow over his disastrous sunset — then against all critics defend me, thou Spirit of Equality, who has spread one royal mantle of humanity over all my kind! Defend me, thou great democratic God! Thou who didst not deny to the imprisoned convict Bunyan the pale, poetic pearl. Thou who didst clothe the mutilated, impoverished arm of old Cervantes in leaves of the finest gold. Thou who didst pluck Andrew Jackson from the dirt and hurl him onto a warhorse, thundering him higher than a throne! Thou who, in all Thy mighty earthly marches, ever choosest Thy finest champions from the common people — defend me, O God!
